And the firstlings of thy herd. The one who is fit to eat them shall eat them, as I have previously explained.

That thou mayest learn. This means that when you go to the revered place, there they [kohanim] will teach you. There is a second meaning to le-ma’an tilmad (that thou mayest learn). Tilmad is similar in meaning to melummadah (well broken), as in And Efraim is a heifer well broken (Hoshea 10:11). Its meaning is habituated. This interpretation appears correct to me.
Then shalt thou turn it into money. The reference is to the tithe.
In thy hand. It is placed in your hands.
Or for strong drink. Made from honey, dates, wheat, or barley.
Or for whatever thy soul asketh of thee. Fruits.

Thou and thy household. You and your sons are obligated. It is optional for your household, for the commandment mandating the three pilgrimages falls on males. The woman who goes to the chosen place, as Elkanah’s wives did, is rewarded.

And the Levi that is within thy gates. The reference is to the house of Levi. You will be rewarded if you do not forsake him. You shall give the Levi what you can afford. The verse probably speaks of the first tithe. Since Scripture mentioned the second tithe, it now goes on to say, do not think that you have fulfilled your obligation with the second tithe alone.

[That is within thy gates.] The meaning of that is within thy gates is that one should give it to the Levi that is within his gates. He should not say, I will keep it with me and give it to another Levi, or that I have given it.

At the end of every three years. The reference is to the third tithe. Bnei Yisrael do not have to give the second tithe this year. Some say that Bnei Yisrael had to give all three tithes. Those who deny the Rabbinic tradition say that the first tithe is the commandment referred to in the verse that begins, Thou shalt surely tithe (v. 1).

They say that thou shalt turn it into money (v. 25) is directed to the Levi and that similarly the firstlings… of thy flock (v. 23) is directed to the kohen. They say there is no such thing as the second tithe except for tithe given in the third year.
At the end. At the beginning. The tithe given in the third year is called the “poor tithe.” We will rely on the tradition of our fathers.

At the end of every seven years.] Its meaning, as I have explained, is, at the beginning of the year. Assemble the people (Devarim 31:12) is proof of this. This section follows because Scripture states that the poor tithe belongs to the Levi, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. Scripture now says that the same applies to the remission of debts (shemittah). The word shemittah is similar to shimtuha (throw her down) (Melachim II 98:33), the meaning of which is, release her and she will fall.

Creditor. The word masheh (loan) follows the paradigm of matteh (rod) (Shemot 4:4). I believe that masheh is a noun. However, many believe that masheh is a verb. The word ba’al (creditor) is similar to be’aleha (him that hath it) in wisdom preserveth the life of him that hath it (Kohelet 7:12) and be’alav (the owners thereof) in It taketh away the life of the owners thereof (Mishlei 1:19). It means the one who has the matter in his power.
That which he hath lent. Yasheh (that which he hath lent) is a transitive verb. The one who borrows is called a nosheh bo (a borrower) (Is. 24:2).

He shall not exact it. The word yiggos (exact) means to press. Compare, tingosu (exact) in and exact all your labors (Is. 58:3). Look, the nun is visible in the imperfect in a word whose stem begins with a nun.

Hashem’s release. In honor of Hashem, who has bestowed wealth upon him. The name of Hashem is connected to the word release because the year of release is called a Sabbath unto Hashem (Vayikra 25:2,4).
Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it. It is optional.

Howbeit. This means that you shall take note that that which I commanded you, not to exact interest from your brother, will be unnecessary if all of Yisrael or most of them will listen to Hashem’s voice. In this case, there will be no poor among you who need you to lend to them. On the contrary, all of you shall lend to many nations (v. 6). The meaning of ve-ha’avateta (and thou shalt lend) (v. 6) is, you shall take his pledge (avot), that is, his pawn, for the money that you shall give him, which he needs to do business.

And thou shalt rule. Furthermore, being upright you will rule over nations. However, there is a commandment stating If there be among you a needy man (v. 7). Moshe knew that a generation will arise that will not be mostly meritorious. He therefore said, For the poor shall never cease out of the land (v. 11).
Thou shalt not harden thy heart. By refraining from addressing comforting words to him.

Shut. Tikpotz means you shall shut. Compare, kafetzah (stoppeth) in kafetzah piha (stoppeth her mouth) (Tehillim 107:42; Iyov 5:16); kafatz be-af (shut up His compassion) (Tehillim 77:10); and yikpetzu (shall shut) in Kings shall shut their mouths (Is. 52:15). Tikpotz is a verb in the kal.

Needy. Some say that the word evyon (needy) is related to the word avah (would) in and he would not (Shemot 10:27), for evyon follows the paradigm elyon, chevy on, and hegyon, the roots of which are ayin, lamed, heh; chet, bet, heh; heh, gimel, heh. An evyon is so called because he desires everything because of his need.
But thou shalt surely open thy hand. Pato’ach (open) is an infinitive. Whenever Scripture omits the infinitive, it is employing an abridged style. The midrashic interpretation is also beautiful.
Open thy hand to him. To the one who has nothing.
And shalt surely lend him. The meaning of veha’avet tavitennu (and shalt surely lend him) is, give him from yours by taking his pledge. Tavitennu means take his pledge.
Base. The word beliya’al (base) is a noun. Some say that beliya’al is a compound. It refers to a prayer that the vile person should not ascend, should not grow, and should not live.

And thine eye be evil. Ve-ra’ah (and thine eye be evil) is similar to ve-shavah (and is returned) in and is returned unto her father’s house (Vayikra 22:13). The word comes from a root two of whose letters are pronounced.

That. Bi-gelal (that) means the same as sibbah (because of). Compare, sabbev (cause) in cause to change (Shmuel II 14:20). For the All is in the parts, that is, in the parts of the All, that is, the body.
Thou shalt surely give him. It means that if you give him, then Hashem will add to your wealth.
For the poor shall never cease out of the land. As I have explained.
Unto thy…brother. First, the one who is close to you.

Unto thy poor. The poor of your family. The needy of your land come before the needy of another place. If thy brother, a Hebrew man (v. 12) follows because of thou shalt furnish him liberally (v. 14).
Thy brother a Hebrew. I have explained this.
Or a Hebrew woman. The reference is to And if a man sell his daughter to be a maid-servant (Shemot 21:7).
Empty. I have explained this.

Thou shalt furnish him liberally. Ha’anek ta’anik (thou shalt furnish him liberally) means treat him gloriously. Ta’anik (thou shalt furnish him) is related to the word anakim (chains) in And chains about thy neck (Mishlei 1:9). On the other hand, the meaning of ta’anik is to be derived from its context. In this case, the word has no brother.

Through his ear and into the door. I have explained this. Scripture mentions this because it states that you are obligated to furnish him liberally when he goes free. However, if the slave does not want to go free, then you shall pierce his ear through with an awl.

And also unto thy bondwoman thou shalt do likewise. This is connected to thou shalt furnish him liberally (v. 14), even though it is some distance from it, for a woman does not have her ear pierced. Compare, He shall make restitution; if he have nothing (Shemot 22:2); And if he do not these three unto her (Shemot 21:11), and many other instances.

It shall not seem hard unto thee. We find it written in Scripture, three years, as the years of a hireling (Is. 16:14). The latter proves that a person has no right to hire himself out for more than three years. The law similarly applies to the one who hires him and pays his wages.

[Double.] The following is the definition of mishneh. It means double. Similarly mishneh (twice) in ve-hayah mishneh (and it shall be twice as much) (Shemot 16:5). The word mishneh in the latter is a noun. However, mishneh (next) in mishneh la-melekh (next unto king) (Esther 10:3) is an adjective. It is also related, as I have explained, to the word shenayin (two). Note, our verse explains that and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing (Shemot 21:2) refers to the beginning of the year. There is also proof of this from the year of release (shemitttah) as well as from the Sabbath day.
And…will bless thee. U-verakhekha (and will bless you) is an imperfect, not a perfect. There is no difference between the perfect and imperfect. The tense can only be determined by the context.
All the firstlings. This is mentioned because of thou shalt do no work with the firstling of thine ox.
Thou shalt eat it. The one who is fit to eat it, as I have previously explained. Scripture mentions this a second time in order to explain the law regarding a blemished firstling.
Thou and thy household. The household of the kohen.
Any ill blemish. That are mentioned.

Within thy gates. Some say that this means that the kohen shall eat it outside of the sanctuary. Others say, since the animal has a blemish it belongs to the Yisraeli. However, this appears far-fetched to me.

The unclean and the clean. The reference is to may eat it. Our verse is to be understood as a call: you, the clean and the unclean. Its meaning is, one is permitted to eat it whether one is clean or unclean. Scripture states this because one who is unclean and eats holy meat is punished with karet (excision). Scripture reads three times in a year (Devarim 16:16) because it here (v. 20) states year by year. Additionally, because the firstling is to be eaten in the sanctuary. The paschal offering is similarly to be eaten in the sanctuary, not outside it.

The month of abiv. It is called the month of Aviv because when Bnei Yisrael went out of the land of Mitzrayim, the first of the barley crop (aviv) appeared in the fields in that month. Those who deny the Rabbinic tradition say that Passover is not to be observed if the first of the barley crop has not appeared. I have previously responded to their nonsense. We will also admit that the Beth Din took the appearance of the first barley crop into consideration. Note that in Hebrew the months have no names. Nisan (Esther 3:7; Nechemyah 2:1), Sivan (Esther 8:9), and also Kislev (Nechemyah 1:1), Tevet (Esther 2:16), and Adar (Esther 3:7), which are mentioned in Scripture, are Kasdi terms. Hence Scripture states, which is the month of Nisan (Ibid.). However, we find Ziv (Melachim I 6:37), Etanim (Melachim I 8:2), and Bul (Melachim I 6:38). The meaning of first is that when you find the first barley ripe, then the first month has arrived, for one starts counting the months from it We do not care about this, whether the year that passed consisted of twelve months or thirteen months. This is the meaning of first. However, the ancients of blessed memory transmitted traditions regarding many other things along with the ripe barley grain. All of their words are true.
By night. He took you from the authority of Paroh. They left Mitzrayim close to night. I will explain it later.
Of the flock. To fulfill the obligation of the paschal sacrifice.

And the herd. For peace offerings. The fact that Scripture says, and three thousand bullocks (Divrei Hayamim II 35:7), after it says, all of them for the passover-offerings, with regard to the lambs and kids (Ibid.), is proof. It similarly tells us that they gave (unto the Levi) for the passover-offerings five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen (Ibid., v. 9). Scripture thus mentions the Passover offerings before it mentions the cattle. It similarly states, thou and thy household (Devarim 14:26). Some say that Scripture commanded that a lamb or a he-goat were to be offered in Mitzrayim. However, Scripture now tells us if one is able to, he may offer cattle. However, the first interpretation is correct.
Thou shalt eat no leavened bread. No leaven shall be present when the paschal offering is slaughtered.
Bread of affliction. For a memorial.
All the days of thy life. Every year.
Which thou sacrificest…at even. The reference is to the flesh of the Passover offering.
At even, at the going down of the sun. I have explained this previously.

At the season that thou camest forth out of Mitzrayim. The reference is to the Passover offering, as Bnei Yisrael left Mitzrayim in the month of Aviv. It is not connected to at the going down of the sun.

And thou shalt roast. I have previously explained that u-vishalta means you shall roast in fire. Compare, And they roasted (va-yevashelu) the passover with fire (Divrei Hayamim II 35:13). Scripture reads u-vishalta to indicate that the Passover offering is not to be eaten raw.

And thou shalt turn in the morning. Those who deny the Rabbinic tradition say that the verse tells the Yisraeli to go to his house and land on the holy day. We will not rely on our own minds when it comes to the commandments. We will rely only on those who transmitted the Torah. Look, we find Scripture stating, On the eighth day he sent the people away (Melachim I 8:66). The latter was a holy day. Another verse says, And on the three and twentieth day of the seventh month he sent the people away unto their tents (Divrei Hayamim II 7:1). Some say that the meaning of unto their tents is, to their tents, which were close by. They went to their lands on the weekday.
And go unto thy tents. Around Yerushalayim. The Yisraeli would then go to his land on the weekday.

Six days. The ancients said six days from the lifting of the sickle. It is possible that and on the seventh day is connected to six days. And on the seventh day was separated from the first half of the verse and placed in the second half of the verse because Scripture wanted to warn against doing work. Scripture does not say all manner of work. The reason for the latter is that only servile work is prohibited. Where Scripture does state all manner of work, it reads, “Save” [that which every man must eat]. When Scripture mentions that one is obligated to offer the Passover sacrifice in the glorious place, it also mentions the second festival (v. 9) and the third festival (v. 13). It does not mention the day of shofar sounding and the tenth day, because the congregation does not gather then in the sanctuary.
After the measure. The samekh of missat (after the measure) receives a dagesh to compensate for the missing nun. Missat is related to the word nes (banner). It means the lifting of the hand.
The freewill-offering of thy hand. For burnt offerings and peace offerings.
And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman. This is connected to thy man-servant and thy maid-servant (v. 11).
After that thou hast gathered in from thy threshing-floor and from thy winepress. Hence this festival is called the feast of ingathering (Shemot 34:22).

Shalt thou keep a feast. Tachog (shalt thou keep a feast) means you shall sacrifice the offering. The reference is to the congregation. On the other hand, it might refer to the individual. The Yisraeli is told to make burnt and peace offerings. Shall bless thee is proof of this. It means do this because Hashem blessed you. Scripture adds all thine increase to explain that the object of bless thee is the produce which the earth will bring forth.
The work of thy hands. Trade and goods produced by craftsmen.
And thou shalt be altogether joyful. There is a commandment to be joyful on the festival of Sukkot. Others say that it means that God will bless you in the future and you will always be happy.
[Altogether.] The meaning of altogether is, you shall always be happy.
And they shall not appear…empty. This is what Scripture means by after the measure of the freewill-offering of thy hand (v. 10).
Before Hashem. I have already explained this.

[Judges.] Even though each and every commandment stands by itself there is, as it were, a midrashic reason for the connection of the sections. The meaning of Judges…is, even though you are obligated to go three times a year to the place of the kohanim who serve in the sanctuary and there inquire regarding the statues and laws, it will not suffice. You must have judges in all of your cities.

Officers. Shoterim (officers) means rulers. It is related to shoter (ruler) in Overseer, or ruler (Mishlei 6:6) and similarly mishtaro (dominion thereof) in the dominion thereof in the earth (Iyov 38:33). The shofetim (judges) judge and the shoterim (officers) force the crooked [to obey the law].
In all thy gates. We find that Yehoshafat acted in this manner.
Tribe by tribe. In all the gates of each and every tribe.
And they shall judge. The reference is to the judges.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment. Scripture speaks to each one of the judges.
Thou shalt not respect persons. I have explained the word takkir (thou shalt respect) in my comments on Ye shall not respect (takkiru) persons in judgment (Devarim 1:17).

Justice, justice. Moshe speaks to the disputants. Moshe repeats the word justice to indicate that one should pursue justice whether one gains or loses. Or the word is repeated to indicate that one should pursue justice as long as one exists; or the word is repeated for emphasis.
That thou mayest live. Moshe speaks to those who are entering the land.

And inherit the land. Moshe speaks to their children. It means, you will keep this inheritance. The first thing that the judge has to be concerned with is widespread pagan practices such as the one referred to in Thou shalt not plant thee an Asherah (v. 21). The Torah states the latter, for such is the practice of pagan worship, as Behind one in the midst (Is. 66:17) shows.

Neither shalt thou set thee up a pillar. For an idol, as which the Lord thy God hateth proves. However, a pillar which is not set up for idol worship is permitted. The most convincing proof of this is found in the portion which opens with the words And Yaakov sent (Bereshit 32:4).
Thou shalt not sacrifice unto Hashem thy Elokim. Look, when Moshe mentions the asherah and the pillar he also mentions that it is prohibited to slaughter any blemished animal to Elokim.
Even any evil thing. Any evil thing explains any blemish.

For that is an abomination. Its meaning is similar to Present it now unto thy governor (Malachi 12:8). The one who offers it is punished. However, no punishment befalls one who does not sacrifice at all, unless he is obligated to bring an offering.

If there be found in the midst of thee. After Moshe mentions that one is prohibited to plant an asherah near an altar which is in public view, he backtracks and warns the individual not to worship idols.

In transgressing his covenant. La’avor brito (in transgressing His covenant) is the reverse of keeping His covenant. I have previously explained grammatically the word vayishtachu (and worshipped), in the Sefer Ha-Yesod.
Other gods. Idols, the work of man.
Or the sun, or the moon, or any of the host of heaven. Which are the work of Elokim.
Which I have commanded not. To serve them, even though they are My works.

Then thou shalt inquire diligently. Hetev (diligently) means very much. Similarly hetev (greatly) in Art thou greatly angry (Yonah 4:9). It is a bit far-fetched to connect hetev to the word tov (good).

And thou shalt stone them. The man or the woman. It is similar to they shall be burnt with fire, both he and they (Vayikra 20:14). Since Scripture says, and it be told thee (v. 4) in secret, and thou hear it (Ibid.) in public, it had to explain that even though it was told to you, and you heard, they shall not be put to death except upon the testimony of two witnesses.

Or three witnesses. Who accept the testimony of two witnesses. So says the Gaon. Look, the Torah does not state whether we accept the testimony of relatives or of a woman or the testimony of an enemy of the deceased. Some say that if two witnesses contradict two witnesses, then a third witnesses determines innocence or guilt. Others say two witnesses from among the wise men and three from the others. We are thus forced to rely on the words of tradition.
The hand of the witnesses. The hand of each one of the witnesses. Similarly and the heart of the people melted (Yehoshua 7:6). There are many other such instances.
So thou shalt put away. I have previously explained the meaning of u-vi’arta (so thou shalt put away).

If there arise a matter too hard for thee. Moshe speaks to the judges. This follows the previous law because two witnesses are required in order to execute a person. The meaning of between blood and blood is, between innocent blood and guilty blood.
The word yippale (too hard) is similar to the word hayippale (is anything too hard) (Bereshit 18:14). I have explained it there.
Between plea and plea. With regard to money.
And between stroke and stroke. Such as wounds and bruises. Even matters of controversy is a general term.
Then thou shalt arise, and get thee up. I have explained this before.
The priests the Leviyim. For, as I have explained, there are kohanim who are not descended from Levi.
And unto the judge. The reference is to the king who writes a copy of the Torah from the one which is in the hands of the kohanim.
And unto the judge. In the place where he is.
According to the law which they shall teach thee. With regard to the matter that is too hard for you.

Even that man shall die. The court shall put him to death. The reason for the latter is so that the people shall hear, and fear (v. 13). When Moshe mentions the judge, he explains the laws that the judge must keep.
Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee. This is optional.
Whom the Lord thy God shall choose. Via a prophet or via the urim (Shemot 28:30). The point of the clause is you shall not choose him.
Thou mayest not. From a rational point of view.

Who is not thy brother. Who is not of the family of Yisrael, and also one who is an Edomi even though Scripture refers to Edomim as “your brother.” Now in those days horses were brought from Mitzrayim. Scripture’s words concerning Shlomo, And a chariot came up and went out of Mitzrayim (Melachim I 10:29), is proof of this. The king would thus cause Yisrael to sin if he wanted to multiply his horses, for he would cause the people to return to Mitzrayim. This is clearly so: Hashem took Yisrael out of Mitzrayim, and by going back they would desecrate Hashem’s name. Uriyah the prophet fled to Mitzrayim because his life was in danger. Also Yirmiyahu went to Mitzrayim against his will.

Ye shall henceforth return no more. This was a commandment that was not written down. Some say that this law is derived from ye shall see them again no more for ever (Shemot 14:13). However, the latter has a different meaning.
That his heart turn not away. For he will go after his lusts.

Neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold. So that he does not punish Yisrael. Now Yisrael complained about Shlomo who, because of his great love of money, made silver to be in Yerushalayim as stones (Melachim I 10:27). They said [to his son], Thy father made our yoke grievous (Melachim I 12:10). Some say that they complained because of the buildings. However, this is not so, for strangers built the house. The latter is clearly stated in Scripture. Look, following Shlomo’s death Adinoram, who was over the levy, was stoned to death by Bnei Yisrael (Melachim I 10:18).
And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne. At the beginning of his kingship.
A copy. The meaning of mishneh is a second rendition.
it [feminine] will be with him i.e., the Torah [feminine].
he will read it [masculine] i.e., the book [masculine].
He will personally revere; ...
whereas observe all the words means that he will enforce observance upon others.
that he may not be haughty which would occur, if he were above the law.
that he may not turn away for if he did not study, he would not know the law. His reward will be that he lengthen the days .

The priests the Leviyim, even all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion. When Scripture mentions the laws of the king, who is the judge, it makes mention of the laws of the kohanim, who are the teachers of the Torah. After Scripture states that they have no inheritance, it states that they will take from the sacrificer the shoulder, the cheeks, and the maw: the shoulder from the body; the cheeks, which have the tongue between them, from the head; and the maw from the insides. There is a midrashic interpretation that since the kohen slaughters the peace offerings, he receives the shoulder as payment for the use of his shoulder in the slaughtering, the cheeks as payment for reciting the blessing, and the maw as payment for the investigation. However, according to the plain meaning of the text, these are better than the rest of the meat. Scripture also mentions the laws regarding the Leviyim, for they too will teach the Torah in the gates. The Book of Divrei Hayamim shows this to be the case.

Beside that which is his due. Some say that mimkarav (which is his due) is similar to makkarekhem (them that bestow it upon you) in from them that bestow it upon you (Melachim II 12:8). However, they are a bit off the mark. The rules of grammar will not accede to it. On the contrary, mimkarav is related to timkeru mimkar (sell aught) in and if thou sell aught (Vayikra 25:14). The meaning of le-vad mimkarav al ha-avot (beside that which is due according to the father’s house) is, if the kohen sold his house, which he inherited from his father as Scripture states, then the house that was sold in the city of his possession, shall go out (Vayikra 25:33). The latter explains according to the fathers. The local kohanim shall not say to him, Look, you have money, you shall not in addition eat the sacred food with us. On the contrary, they shall eat like portions. After Moshe concludes the laws pertaining to the judge and the kohen, he mentions the laws regarding the prophet.
One that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire. This was a form of idol worship, for we have among us today many gentiles who worship the fire.

Anyone that useth divination. Kosem (one that useth divination) is most probably a general term. It refers to those who issue decrees and declare things will undoubtedly be so. The term gazerin (magicians) is similar. The word kesem (divine sentence) in A divine sentence is in the lips of the king (Mishlei 16:10) is close in meaning to it. The particulars are a soothsayer (me’onen), or an enchanter (menachesh), or a sorcerer (mechashef). It is also possible that kosem is a specific term for astrologers and that kesamim (divinations) refers to divination that astrologers make based on the primary and secondary stars.
A soothsayer, or an enchanter. I have explained these terms previously.
Or a sorcerer. I have also explained this term.
Or a charmer. One who calls the demons together.
Or one that consulteth a ghost or a familiar spirit. I have explained these terms before.

Or a necromancer. Such as those who go to cemeteries and take the bone of a dead person and, because of their imagination and madness, see shapes while they are awake or in a dream. All of these things are abominations to Hashem. The truth is that a person must fully believe in his creator in his heart. When a person relies on his wisdom, and not on Hashem, in seeking the truth and what will be in the future, his mind is deficient, for it is perverted. The person who wants to inquire, let him inquire from Hashem via a prophet. Scripture therefore afterward reads, A prophet will Hashem…raise up…from the midst of thee (v. 15). The latter refers to Yehoshua. Unto him ye shall hearken (Ibid.), which is later followed by and the children of Yisrael hearkened unto him (Devarim 34:9), is proof of this. The fact that we do not find any other prophet but Yehoshua entering Kenaan is additional proof of this. It is also possible that our verse lays down a general rule for each and every prophet who will arise after Moshe.
Like unto me. Who is a prophet of Hashem and not an enchanter.

I will require it of him. His death is thus caused by Hashem. What happened to the man who did not listen to the words of the prophet who said, Smite me, I pray thee (Melachim I 20:35) is proof of this. Scripture states there that the prophet spoke by the word of Hashem (Melachim I 21:35), The prophet was previously known as a prophet of Hashem.

When a prophet speaketh. The prophet Yirmiyahu similarly says, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass (Yirmiyahu 28:9) in the time predicted by the prophet. After Moshe finished explaining the law relating to the soothsayers and their practices, which were practiced by the idolaters of the land, he warned that no innocent blood be shed in the land. The reason for this is that the land shall be pure from the abomination of the soothsayers, and it should also not be defiled by the shedding of innocent blood.
Thou shalt prepare thee the way. The cities should be in a place where the way is prepared and settled.
And divide. Ve-shillashta (and divide) means divide the land into three, or place a city of refuge in each third of the land.
His neighbor. Et re’ehu means with his neighbor. There are many such cases.
Fetcheth a stroke. Ve-niddechah (fetcheth a stroke) is a nifal. Nidche (the dispersed of) in He gathereth together the dispersed of Yisrael (Tehillim 147:2) is the kal form.
With the axe. Garzen (axe) refers to a metal instrument used to cut a tree down. It is related to the word nigzarti (I was cut off).

And the head slippeth from the helve. Venashal (slippeth) is similar to ve-nasa (shall set forward) (Bamidbar 2:17). It is related to the word yishal (shall drop off) in for thine olives shall drop off (Devarim 28:40). The word ve-nashal (and shall cast) in and shall cast out many nations (Devarim 7:1) is transitive. However, ve-nashal (slippeth) in our verse is intransitive. According to a great grammarian the same is true of the word yasaf (more) in with a great voice, and it went on no more (Devarim 5:19) and yasaf (added) in For Hashem hath added sorrow (Yirmiyahu 45:3). However, I believe that they are both transitive.
And smite him mortally. Ve-hikkahu nefesh (and smite him mortally) is short for ve-hikkahu makkat nefesh (and smite him with a mortal blow). He will strike him in a place where his soul will depart.

And if Hashem thy Elokim enlarge thy border. If Yisrael observes the entire Torah. Scripture therefore reads, if thou shalt keep all this commandment (v. 9), the reference being to the commandment dealing with the three cities of refuge.
And to walk ever in his ways. Without any break in them.

Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmarks. The meaning of tassig (thou shalt…remove) is known. Its meaning is similar to the word tasseg (remove) in Remove not the ancient landmark (Mishlei 22:28). It is close in meaning to destroyed.
Which they of old time have set. The ones who divided up the land.

One witness shall not rise up. This section follows, because destroying the boundary markers leads to quarrels, blows, and murder. Scripture therefore goes on to state, following this, Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth (v. 21). The one who claims that his neighbor removed his landmark must bring witnesses. Hence, Scripture reads, one witness shall not rise up, which means that two witnesses are required in cases involving murder, assault, landmark removal, or any matter. Shene edim (two witnesses) is an abridged phrase, for Scripture elsewhere reads, shenayim edim (two witnesses) (Devarim 17:6).
To bear perverted witness against him. Such as accusing him of idol worship.
Testified. Anah means testified. The same law applies to flogging and fines.
And thine eye shall not pity. This means thine eye shall not pity the false witness.

When thou goest forth to battle. This is connected to And thine eye shall not pity (Devarim 19:21), for one is not to have pity. However, when going forth to war you should pity the man who has betrothed a woman, or built a house, or planted a vineyard, or one whose heart is faint.
That the priest shall approach. The kohen who has been anointed for war.
Fear not. In your heart.
Nor be alarmed. And flee.
Neither be ye affrighted. In deed.

Dedicated it. Chanakho (dedicated it) is similar to the word chanukkat (dedication of) in the dedication offer of the altar (Bamidbar 7:10). The word chanokh (train) in Train up a child (Mishlei 22:6) is similar. Our rabbis, of blessed memory, learned from the latter that we train (mekhannechin) children. The reason that [one who has not dedicated his house is released from service] is that such a man’s heart and desire is to dedicate his house. Look, his mind will be upon his house, not on the battle. He will therefore flee and cause others to flee.
Used the fruit thereof. The word chillelo (used the fruit thereof) is connected to the word challilim (flutes), for they were in the habit of dancing in the vineyards (Jud. 21:21).

And what man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? In marriage. Look, this verse is a sign that there are people who die when their time comes. However, the one who dies in battle dies before his time. Hence David said, or he shall go down into battle, and be swept away (Shmuel I 26:10).
That is fearful. To strike another person.
And faint-hearted. To suffer someone’s blow.
His brethren’s heart. Look, the word et appears superfluous. However, its meaning is as I have previously explained. It indicates the thing itself.
Shall be appointed. U-fakedu (shall be appointed) is related to the word pekod (appoint).
Then proclaim peace unto it. The meaning of ve-karata is proclaim unto it. This is a commandment, or it is most likely an option.
And if it will make no peace. The meaning of tashlim is, it will make peace.
Which are very far off from thee. Who are not of the seven nations.

Thou shalt save alive nothing. It is forbidden to give them food or drink. The general rule is that they were to kill them if possible. The latter applied to their days. Moshe does not mention the Girgashi, for they were the least and the smallest among them.

For is the tree of the field man. I have previously explained in the Sefer Ha-Yesod that it is possible in all languages to be brief and to apply an abbreviated style, as in “an ass bread” (Shmuel I 16:20). However, it is impossible to leave out the word lo (no, not), for in this case the meaning would be reversed. A great Spanish grammarian said that a heh has been omitted. Our clause should be interpreted as if written, hakhi adam etz ha-sadeh (for is the tree of the field man). Now this interpretation does not appear correct to me. Why would Scripture say that you shall not destroy fruit trees, because, unlike a human being, they cannot run away from you? I believe there is no need for all this. The following is the meaning of our clause. For thou mayest eat of them, but thou shalt not cut them down, for the tree of the field is man; that is, the life of man is supported by trees. Compare, For he taketh a life to pledge (Devarim 24:6), which is short for, for he taketh that which sustains man’s life to pledge.

But thou shalt not cut them down. This is connected to that it should he besieged of thee. Look, do not destroy a fruit tree, which is a source of sustenance for human life. Be that as it may, you are permitted to eat of it but you are prohibited from destroying it so that the city will be besieged because of you. The fact that Scripture then states thou mayest destroy and cut down, that thou mayest build bulwarks (v. 20), is proof of this.
Until it fall. Scripture would not have said a long time (v. 19) if the city were not mighty.

If one be found slain. As Scripture mentions the war against enemies, it goes on to say what the law is if one fights against his fellow and a corpse is found in the land of Yisrael, and the one who slew him is unknown.
Thy elders. The elders and judges of the cities that are close to the body.
A heifer of the herd, which hath not been wrought with. Never used for plowing.
And which hath not drawn in the yoke. To bring stones, as is the practice with heifers.
Rough. The word etan (rough) means mighty.
And shall break…the neck. Ve-arefu (and they shall break) means they shall remove the back of the neck of the heifer.
And the priests the sons of Levi shall come near. The priests (kohanim) who are clearly of the sons of Levi.
And according to their word shall…be. The punishment for every controversy and every stroke.
And all the elders of that city. The elders referred to in then thy elders…shall come forth (v. 2).

[Shed.] The heh in shafekhu (shed) indicates the plural. It is like the heh in shafekhu ashurai (my steps slipped) (Tehillim 73:2). However, interpreting it midrashically, the heh refers to each one of the hands, for the word yad (hand) is in most cases feminine.

Neither have our eyes seen it. It is possible that Hashem commanded the city closest to the slain to perform this because if the city had not committed a similar deed, then the murder of a person near their city would not have occurred. Hashem’s thoughts are deep and infinitely beyond our comprehension.
And they shall speak and say. Ve-anu ve-ameru (and they shall speak and say) is similar to ve-anita ve-amarta (and thou shalt speak and say) (Devarim 26:5). I will explain it there.
Forgive, o Lord, thy people. Who erred and did not guard the dangerous roads.

Shall be forgiven. A tav has been omitted in the word ve-nikapper (shall be forgiven). It is similar to the word venivasseru (may be taught) in that all women may be taught (Yechezkel 23:48). They are a combination of two forms, the nifal and the hitpa’el.

Scripture mentions whom thou hast redeemed to indicate that as You redeemed Yisrael from Mitzrayim as a manifestation of Your great mercies, similarly redeem them from this blood and the punishment for its shedding.

So shalt thou put away the innocent blood. The meaning of the innocent blood is, the punishment for the shedding of the innocent blood. On the other hand, the word ha-dam ha-naki (the innocent blood) is short for ha-dam, dam ha-naki (the blood, the innocent blood). Some say that the meaning of so shalt thou put away the innocent blood is, you must eradicate the shedding of blood. However, in my opinion, and I have mentioned this before, it means no innocent blood will be shed in your land if you do what is right in the eyes of Hashem. The latter is in keeping with the secret that the reward of sin is sin, and the reward of a commandment is the commandment.

When thou goest forth to battle. This section is connected with When thou shalt besiege a city (Devarim 20:19). The section dealing with the decapitated heifer was inserted between them because it deals with a slain person found in the Land of Yisrael. This law does not apply outside of the Land of Yisrael and certainly not in time of war.
A woman. The rabbis have already explained this.
Of goodly form. In his own eyes.
And thou hast a desire unto her. You will desire to take her for a wife, for after this Scripture states, and be her husband. So I took her to be my wife (le-ishah) (Bereshit 12:19) is similar.
Then thou shalt bring her home to thy house; and she shall shave her head. Some say that she shaves her head as he may have desired her because of her hair.
Pare. Ve-asetah et tzipparneha (and pare her nails) means she shall let her nails grow long so that she will appear disgusting in his eyes.
And she shall put the raiment of her captivity from off her. For he may have desired her because of her beautiful garments.
And bewail. So that he is no longer happy with her.
A full month. Perhaps his desire will cool. Others say: SHE SHALL SHAVE HER HEAD. Because she is unclean. The law regarding the leper is similar.

And pare. Ve-asetah (and pare) means and fix. Its fixing consists in cutting off the excess. Compare, asah (trimmed) in nor trimmed his heard (Shmuel II 19:25) and in And instead of curled hair (ma’aseh miksheh) baldness (Is. 3:24). The main meaning of the word ma’aseh (work) in Scripture is fixing, except for instances when something unseemly follows. However, even in the latter instance the reference might be to complete an evil deed.
And she shall put the raiment of her captivity from off her. For it is filthy.
And shall remain in thy house, and be wail…a full month. This means she shall remain in your house a month to cry.

Her father and her mother. If close by. Some say that she bewails her father and mother because they did not convert to Judaism. However, I believe that reason teaches us that every person is obligated to honor his father and his mother while they live and also after their deaths.

The meaning of and bewail… is, she shall mourn her parents if they were killed while she was taken captive in the same manner that a Yisraeli women mourns, for she is converting to Judaism. Scripture had no need to mention that she shall bathe, for it is necessary for her to be purified by the waters of sprinkling, as Scripture earlier states, ye and your captives (Bamidbar 31:19).

[And after that thou mayest go into her, and be her husband.] Our rabbis, of blessed memory, said that he has to wait three months. Even though the words of our sages need no support I offer the following as proof, And it came to pass about three months after (Bereshit 38:24). The latter is the time when the fetus begins to move. It is prohibited to have sexual relations with a women when one is in doubt as to whether she is pregnant or not, because of the uncertain paternity of the fetus; for some women give birth two months short of the normal term. Others give birth later than the normal term. However, the latter rarely occurs.
A full month. Yerach yamim (a full month) is similar to chodesh yamim (a whole month) (Bamidbar 11:21). I have explained this previously. A month is called a yerach because the moon is its basis.
Then thou shalt let her go. You shall do to her as she desires.
But thou shalt not sell her at all for money. Scripture speaks of what is widely practiced. Its true meaning is, do not sell her.

Thou shalt not deal with her as with a slave. The word titammer (deal as with a slave) is similar to the word ve-hitammer (and he deal as with a slave) in and he deal with him as a slave (Devarim 24:7). The word is not found a third time. The meaning of the word has to be ascertained from its context. It means deceitfully.
Beloved. In his eyes, not in the eyes of God.
That was hated. Seni’ah (hated) is an adjective. This section follows because the preceding section reads, and thou hast a desire unto her (v. 11) and…if thou have no delight in her (v. 14).
In the day that he causeth his sons to inherit. When he is in good health; or on the day of his demise when he is deathly ill; or the law courts cause his sons to inherit.
Make…first-born. In word and in status.
[That he may not.] Lo yukhal (that he may not) is to be understood like its counterparts.

He shall acknowledge. He shall acknowledge him by an act, or he shall admit before others who the firstborn is, if the first-born is in a place where he is unknown, or he is obligated right at the beginning to acknowledge which one of his sons is the first-born should they be twins.

By giving him a double portion. The first-born shall take two parts. If there are three sons let them imagine that there are four and the first-born shall take two parts. If there are two sons let them imagine that there are three, and so in all cases. In my opinion this too is the meaning of I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me (Melachim II 2:9), as I explained in its place.
For he is the first-fruits of his strength. The one known as first-born. Scripture speaks of the upright. All of Yisrael are presumed to be upright.
Stubborn and rebellious. Towards Hashem and towards the parents if they be Hashem-fearing.
Stubborn. The word soreh (stubborn) is similar to the word sorre’ah (stubborn) in like a stubborn heifer (Hoshea 4:16). He does not keep the positive commandments.
And rebellious. With regard to the negative commandments.
And though they chasten him. In the presence of witnesses. The parents are commanded to take hold of him and bring him [to the elders]. The words of tradition are true.

He is a glutton. The meaning of zolel (glutton) is explained. It refers to one who gluttonously devours meat. However, the term refers to anyone who commits himself to all that he lusts for, to all that his desires ask of him.

And a drunkard. Sove refers to one who drinks a lot. It refers to a drunkard. This individual is essentially a heretic. He desires life in this world only for eating and drinking. This portion was placed here because of the woman of goodly form. And his mother’s name was Shlomit (Vayikra 24:11) and the hint which I gave with reference to the sons of Aharon are proof of this.
And thou hang him. We have received from the rabbis, of blessed memory, traditions regarding those who are hanged.

For he that is hanged is a reproach unto Elokim. For he cursed Hashem. However, according to the plain meaning of the text, Elokim is the subject. The curse comes to all places close to the hanged. It has a secret connected to the soul. Scripture therefore goes on to say, that thou defile not thy land. This section follows because of the war, for Scripture first states, When thou goest forth to battle (Devarim 20:1). Now the incident at Givon shows that the purpose of the law which says that his body shall not remain upon the tree all night is not out of respect for the deceased but rather out of respect for the land, for the law of the Kenaani and the law of Bnei Yisrael differ.
Thou shalt not see thy brother’s ox. Even when you go out to war. This is midrashic.
And hide thyself. This is connected to Thou shalt not see. Scripture mentions the ox and the sheep (v. 1). The ass was previously mentioned (Shemot 23:4). The same law applies to all beasts.
Then thou shalt bring it home. If you are coming back or you command someone; that is, you give it to an honest person for safekeeping.
Thou mayest not. Lo tukhal (thou mayest not) is to be understood like its counterparts.
Fallen down. Nofelim (fallen down) means crouching. The word nofelim is a general term.
Thou shalt surely help him to lift them up again. Not by yourself. Compare, thou shalt surely release it with him (Shemot 23:5).

A woman shall not wear that which pertaineth unto a man. This law was stated here because Scripture deals with going out to war. Women were created only to have children. If a woman joins men in going to war she will come to engage in illicit sexual relations on the way. The law that states neither shall a man put on a woman’s garment is similar. The reason for this law is as follows. If a male who does not have a full beard mixes with women, then he and they will have sexual relations without anyone knowing. This law indicates that the custom of Yisrael was for the garments of men to be unlike the garments of women. There was a definite difference between the garments. This is also the practice in most countries. Some say that our verse speaks of unnatural intercourse. However, there is no need for this interpretation. The fact is that Hashem abominates the one who changes the works of Hashem.
If a bird’s nest chance to be before thee in the way. This section follows because Scripture earlier mentioned by the way (v. 4).
Chance. The word yikkare (chance) is similar to nikro nikreti (As I happened by chance) (Shmuel II 1:6). These words have the meaning of chance. It is close in meaning to “meet.”

[Young ones.] The alef in efrochim (young ones) is superfluous. It is like the alef of u-ve-ezro’akha (and with your arm) (Yirmiyahu 32:21). It is very cruel to crush a mother with her children. Hence the reason for this law. The same applies to an ox or a sheep.
That it may be well with thee. For Hashem will pity you and do good things for you.
And that thou mayest prolong thy days. As you did not exterminate all of the nest but left its root.
When thou buildest a new house. This section is placed here because it deals with Yisrael in its land after they wage war. Scripture opens with the law dealing with a house.

A parapet. The meaning of ma’akeh (parapet) is known from its context. It has no neighbor. A grammarian connected it to the word akat (oppression of) in the oppression of the wicked (Tehillim 55:4). However, he oppressed himself.

If any man fall. Scripture speaks of the end result. The following are similar: The dead shall be put to death (Devarim 17:6); And stripped the naked of their garments (Iyov 22:6); And the children struggled together (Bereshit 25:22). There are an innumerable number of words that are named because of the end result. We do not know if this is linguistic style or prophetic statements, as in and pursued as far as Dan (Bereshit 14:14); unto the valley of Eshkol (Bamidbar 13:23); and Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother (Bereshit 2:24). After laying down the law dealing with the house, Scripture goes on to deal with the laws of seeds and plants, for after entering the land the Yisraeli would build a house and then plant.

Thou shalt not sow thy vineyard. The following is the meaning of pen tikdash (lest the fullness): Rabbi Menachem ben Saruk the Sephardi has already explained in his notebook that the word tikdash (fullness) is related to the word kodesh (holy). [The product of two seeds sown together becomes holy] because one mixes with the other.

Thou shalt not plow with an ox and an ass. This law is connected to the one dealing with sowing two kinds of seed. Hashem had mercy on his creatures. An ass is not as strong as an ox. The law prohibiting the mixture of linen and wool follows because Scripture earlier mentioned the prohibition of mixing seeds. This law was previously mentioned in general terms. However, Scripture is specific here. It limits the prohibition to wool and linen, and not to any other kinds of material.

Thou shalt make twisted cords. The deniers say that this is a separate commandment pertaining to nighttime. It is similar to the fringes that are to be worn during the day. Scripture therefore reads, wherewith thou coverest thyself. However, the transmitters of tradition say that our verse speaks of the fringes that are to be worn during the day. The meaning of gedilim (twisted cords) is similar to the word gedilim (wreaths) which is employed with regard to the building of the temple. Compare, wreaths (gedilim) of chainwork (Melachim I 7:17). The deniers connect the word gedilim to the word gedolah (large). We believe only in the words of our ancestors. Scripture mentions this law a second time in order to add upon the four corners. The law mandating fringes is connected to the law prohibiting a mixture of linen and wool because the latter does not apply to fringes.

If any man take a wife. According to the deniers this section was connected to the law of fringes because the latter contain the phrase wherewith thou coverest thyself. Its true reason can be explained midrashically. The laws are placed one next to the other because first comes the house, next a garment, and then the mistress of the house.
Wanton. The word alilot (wanton) means a cause.
Charges. Whether true or false.
Virginity. The word betulim (virginity) is a plural. It never comes in the singular. The same applies to bacharut (youth), zekunim (old age), alumim (youth).
The father of the damsel, and her mother. If they are alive. Otherwise, someone appointed by the court.
[He may not put her away all his days.] The meaning of all his days is that she shall always be under his care. She shall be so until the day of his death.

Shall stone her. Someone most likely slept with her after he betrothed her, for the one who betrothed her would not have done so unless she told him that she was a virgin. The transmitters of the law explained the matter very clearly. The signs of virginity are found until a fixed time, according to the nature of young ladies. The law dealing with a married women was connected to the law of the betrothed damsel because Scripture states, and the men of the city shall stone her.
Both of them. The meaning of gam is this one like the other one. Now Scripture goes on to further elucidate this topic.
If there be. When this thing shall happen.
The gate. The place where the elders of the city sit. Look, Scripture refers to the betrothed woman as his neighbor’s wife. We cannot ascertain the meaning of betrothal except through tradition.
Unto the damsel…do nothing.] She most probably did not agree and was unaware until he came and raped her. Hence the rapist is compared to a murderer.
Cried. She most likely cried.
That is not betrothed. Our verse deals with rape, not with seduction.
A man shall not take his father’s wife. The woman whom his father raped. This section therefore follows.

He that is crushed. Dakkah (crushed) refers to the testicles. The word does not appear again in Scripture. The grammarians say that it refers to the flesh, which is soft. However, this is far-fetched.
Privy parts. Shofkhah (privy parts) refers to the organ from which urine and semen pour.

Into the assembly of Hashem. It means that they shall not be considered as part of Hashem’s assembly with regard to taking a daughter of Yisrael. Similarly, an Amoni male to the exclusion of an Amoni female, and a Moavi male to the exclusion of a Moavi female. Rut is the true witness to the latter. The verse that says neither shall they come among you (Melachim I 11:2) speaks of the women of the seven nations. Furthermore, the verse in the Book of Ezra which states, that they separated from Yisrael all the alien mixture (Nechemyah 13:3), refers to the males. I have explained it there.

Our rabbis, of blessed memory, said that a mamzer (bastard) is a child that results from a sexual act which is deemed an uncovering of the nakedness. The two mems of mamzer are superfluous. They are like the mems in mamgurot (barns) in the barns are broken down (Yoel 1:17). Others say that mamzer is the name of a people. Compare, And a mamzer shall dwell in Ashdod (Zecharyah 9:6), for it is far-fetched for Yisrael to be given a shameful name. It is even more unlikely for this to happen in the time of the salvation. The Aramaic translator of the Bible was brief and midrashic.
But Hashem thy Hashem turned. For Bilam intended to curse. However, Hashem did not permit him to do so.

When thou goest forth in camp. The reference is to a camp which goes out to fight the enemy accompanied by the ark. Scripture speaks of a small camp. The Torah does not speak of the great camp, for this camp had built partitions. When Yisrael went to war they were close to and around the ark. It is clear that a person who is unclean because of a nocturnal event destroys his seed. This section follows because of the Midyani war, for Scripture mentioned the topic of Bilam. The Midyanim assailed Yisrael because of the affair of their sister. The ark was with the camp that went out to fight the Midyanim.
From every evil thing. Spiritually or physically, such as ejaculations.
Chanceth. The mem of mi-kereh (chanceth) is a preposition. Mi-kereh follows the paradigm of mi-sedeh (part of the field) in part of the field of his possession (Vayikra 27:16).

When evening cometh on. Li-fenot erev (when evening cometh) is similar in meaning to ki fanah ha-yom (for the day declineth) (Yirmiyahu 6:4). This also strengthens the opinion of the rabbis of blessed memory. The deniers say that li-fenot (cometh on) means before. They say nothing of value. Some say that the meaning of li-fenot erev (when evening cometh) is, when the evening begins to come. Now, after Scripture employs the phrase li-fenot erev, it says, and when the sun is down. Li-fenot erev thus means before the evening. Li-fenot boker (when the morning appeared) is similarly before sunrise.

A place. The word yad means a place. Compare, yad ha-yarden (by the side of the Yarden) (Bamidbar 13:29). This too is proof [that Scripture speaks of a small camp], for none of the following had to leave the camp of Yisrael: one who experienced an ejaculation, one who had to tend to his bodily needs, and certainly no children. Proof of this is the verse which states, that they put out of the camp every leper, and every one that hath an issue, and whosoever is unclean by the dead (Bamidbar 5:2), which refers to uncleanliness that is passed on and not to one who is unclean for a day.
[Thy weapons.] The alef of azenekha (thy weapons) is superfluous. Azenekha is related to the word zonot (weapons) in and the weapons washed (Melachim I 22:38).
And cover that which cometh from thee. For all disgusting things which are visible to the eye give birth to a defect in the soul.
No unseemly thing. In deed or speech.
And turn away from thee. Its meaning is that God will not go before you, for the latter is clearly stated.
Thou shalt not deliver…a bondman. It is possible that when Yisrael goes to war, a non-Israelite bondman escapes into their camp.

From his master. The master too is not a Yisraeli. The bondman came for the glory of Hashem, whose name is called over Yisrael. If the Yisraeli turns the slave over to his master this will entail the desecration of Hashem’s name. Scripture therefore reads, thou shalt not wrong him.

[There shall be no harlot] The law of the kedeshah (harlot) follows because the previous section deals with a bondman. The transmitters of tradition say that the term kadesh (sodomite) refers to the one who is slept with. The phrase of the sons of Yisrael is proof of this. Elihu said, [Their soul perisheth in youth] And their life as that of the depraved (kedeshim) (Iyov 36:14); their soul corresponds to their life and kedeshim corresponds to in youth. Scripture also states, And there were also sodomites (kadesh) in the land (Melachim I 14:24); the house of the sodomites (kedeshim) Melachim II 23:7). Scripture there continues, where the women wove coverings (Ibid.). I do not understand the meaning of the word kedeshah. (harlot). When we investigate carefully the meaning of the word we find that it refers to a woman who is known to be prepared to offer herself to all who come and go. Where is the harlot (kedeshah) (Bereshit 38:21) is proof of this. If this is so, then the term kadesh refers to an Egyptian-like practice. The intelligent will understand. The law dealing with a harlot’s hire follows because our section deals with a harlot.

Hire. The word etnan (hire) is similar to mattan (gift). The alef is superfluous and the nun is doubled like the peh of na’afufehah (her adulteries) (Hoshea 2:4) and like the resh of the word sagrir (rainy) (Mishlei 27:15). Etnan refers to what the harlot took, that which those who turn to her give her. [The hire of a harlot shall not be brought to the house of God] because it was given for a prohibited act.
Or the price of a dog. For it is a disrespectful act. Scripture therefore goes on to say, for…these are an abomination.

Thou shalt not lend upon interest to thy brother. This law is mentioned here because Scripture earlier mentions the non-Jewish bondman (v. 17). Scripture states that even though it is prohibited to wrong the latter, it is permitted to take interest from him.

Thou shalt not lend upon interest to thy brother. There is a difference between tishokh (you shall take interest) and tashikh (Thou shalt lend upon interest). The meaning of lo tashikh (Thou shalt not lend upon interest) is, you shall not accept interest from your brother when he offers it; your brother also violates the law regarding interest. Notice, tashikh is a word governing two acts. Many say that tashikh is similar to tishokh. There is no difference between them. There are many such verbs in Scripture.
When thou shalt vow a vow. This law follows because Scripture mentioned for any vow when it spoke of the hire of a harlot (v. 19).
For the Lord thy God will surely require it. This is a metaphoric statement. God will act like a person. He will demand what you vowed.
And it will be sin in thee. Chet (sin) means punishment.
That which is gone out of thy lips. Regarding anything where God’s name is mentioned.
Freely. For every vow offering is a free-will offering. However, not every free-will offering is a vow offering. The aforementioned is clear.
Which thou hast promised with thy mouth. After the vow has come out of your mouth you cannot take it back.

When thou comest into thy neighbor’s vineyard. To harvest grapes then you are permitted to eat of them. This section follows to indicate that you are obligated to set aside from your own when taking a vow, but you must not take to yourself that which belongs to another.
In thy vessel. The word kelyekha (thy vessel) is similar to the word edyekha (thy ornaments) (Shemot 33:5).
When thou comest into thy neighbor’s standing corn. To harvest.
Then thou mayest pluck. The word ve-katafta (then thou mayest pluck) is similar to the word ha-kotefim (they pluck) in They pluck salt-wort (Iyov 30:4).
Ears. The meaning of melilot (ears) is known from its context.
A sickle. Chermesh (sickle) is a quadriliteral. The deniers say that this law applies to those who pass by the field, for Scripture says, thou shalt not move a sickle.
When a man taketh a wife. She is also considered fit.
Favor in his eyes. For her nature is the reverse of his.
And he hath found. And he cannot reveal it, for he has no witnesses. The meaning of and he hath found is, or he hath found, as in And he that smiteth his father, or his mother (Shemot 21:15).
And she departeth. She will not return there. It is public knowledge that she left his house permanently.
And becometh. She becomes another man’s wife.
[Another.] The words acher (another) and acharon (latter) (v. 3) are adjectives.
Of divorcement. A bill of divorce is called a sefer keritut because their marriage has been severed forever.

After that she is defiled. With regard to the first husband. Its meaning is defiled to him because another man knew her. The tet of huttamma’ah (she is defiled) receives a dagesh to compensate for the missing tav of the hitpa’el. Similarly the word hukkabbes (is washed) in after that the plague is washed (Vayikra 13:55).
And thou shalt not cause the land to sin. This is a command to Yisrael.

A new wife. Some say a virgin. According to many its meaning is new to him, for it is possible for a man to remarry the woman whom he has divorced if she has not been defiled. Scripture therefore reads a new wife.
He shall be free for his house. The yoke of the king shall not be upon him.
Free. Naki (free) is similar to naki (innocent) in him that is innocent (Iyov 22:30).
[With any business.] The lamed placed before le-khol davar (with any business) is superfluous. It is like the lamed in le-avshalom (Avshalom) in the third, Avshalom (Divrei Hayamim I 3:2).

No man shall take the mill or the upper millstone to pledge. The deniers say that this section is connected to and shall cheer his wife whom he hath taken (v. 5), for our verse alludes to coitus, namely, that it is forbidden to abstain from sexual intercourse. However, this is sheer nonsense. They offer as proof, Then let my wife grind unto another (Iyov 31:10). I have previously explained the latter. The truth is that our verse is to be taken at face value, that a person is prohibited from taking a mill to pledge. The word chovel (one who takes a pledge) is missing from our verse. It is similar to and he said to Yosef (Bereshit 48:1) and to whom she bore to Levi (Bamidbar 26:29), for the meaning of the former is, someone said to Yosef, and of the latter, the one who bore, bore to Levi. There are many such cases.
The mill. The word rechayim (mill) is in the dual form. It does not come in the singular.

The upper millstone. Rechev (upper millstone) refers to a water mill. Others say that it refers to the wood which is placed on the mill. Still others say that the rechayim (mill) refers to the lower millstone and rechev to the upper millstone.

For he taketh a man’s life to pledge. For life is sustained by these instruments. Those who rely on the juxtaposition of the sections have no argument, for each commandment stands by itself. The explanation of their juxtapositions is midrashic. This section is connected to the previous ones in the following way: the Torah mentions that one is not to steal grapes by putting them in his pots (Devarim 23:25), or to lift up a sickle upon his neighbor’s grain (Devarim 23:26); or to take a woman after she has been his and then left his house and married another (v. 1). It also states that one has to cheer the woman whom he marries (v. 5); he is not to be oppressed by going into the army (Ibid.). The taking of a millstone in pledge is a form of oppression. So too is kidnapping a person. Similarly the plague of leprosy, for if he does not observe its laws then the plague will injure those in proximity to it. Scripture similarly states, do not oppress a poor person by taking a pledge from him (v. 10). It similarly states do not oppress a hired person (v. 14) and small children should not be put to death for the sins of the fathers (v. 16). It likewise warns against perverting the justice due a stranger or the fatherless (v. 17). It prohibits the taking of a widow’s garment as a pledge (v. 17). It prohibits one from retrieving a sheaf which was forgotten in the field, for it belongs to the poor (v. 19). Similarly Thou shalt not glean (v. 21). Likewise lest if he should exceed…Then thy brother should be dishonored (Devarim 25:3). The muzzling of an ox (v. 4) is an act of oppression, for the animal toils but cannot eat of its toil. Similarly, refusing to perform levirate marriage (Devarim 25:5-10) is a form of oppression. The woman who grabs a man’s testicles (Devarim 25:11) commits an act of oppression. Employing diverse weights and diverse measures (Devarim 25:13,14) is oppression in its purest form. Furthermore, Amalek oppressed Yisrael (Devarim 25:17-19).
Any of his brethren. Scripture adds of the children of Yisrael because the Edomim are called brothers.
And he deal with him as a slave. The word vehitammer (and he deal with him as a slave) is to be explained as its counterpart.
The priests the Leviyim. The kohanim who are members of the tribe of Levi.
Unto Miriam. Here is proof of the midrashic statement that we should not read the word metzora as metzora (a leper) but as an acronym for motzi shem ra (one who invents libel).
Dost lend. The word tasheh (thou…dost lend) comes from the root nun, shin, heh.
The heh of the word me’umah (any manner of loan) is superfluous. It is like the heh of laylah (night).
To fetch. To take his pledge.

And it shall be righteousness unto thee. You shall weigh your neighbor in the righteous scales which you possess so that he sleeps with his pledge. According to the transmitters of tradition there are places wherein there is a difference between the word tzedek (righteousness) and tzedakah (righteousness).
[The pledge.] I have previously explained the meaning of the pledge in the Torah portion Now These Are the Ordinances (Shemot 21:1) in my comments on “his garment” (Shemot 22:26).
In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it. A negative commandment follows the positive commandment for emphasis.
Upon it. His wages
Setteth his heart. To sustain himself from it. He therefore hired himself out.

[The fathers shall not be put to death.] Those whose spirits wander ask: “How could Scripture say: The fathers shall not he put to death…when it says in another place, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children (Shemot 20:5; Devarim 5:9)?” Their question is nonsense, for the fathers shall not he put to death for the children is a commandment directed to Yisrael. However, God is the one who metes out punishment in visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children. I have earlier explained this in its place.

But thou shalt remember. Scripture mentioned the stranger for this reason, namely, that you do not pervert the justice due him. Moshe previously mentioned some of the laws to the fathers. He also repeated them to the children.
That Hashem…may bless thee. For you gave what you thought was yours but Hashem will give you what is truthfully His.

When thou beatest. Tachbot (thou beatist) is similar to chovet (beating) in beating out wheat (Jud. 6:11). It is in the pa’al. The word yechavet (is beaten) in But the black cummin is beaten (Is. 28:27) is a nifal. All letters whose first root letter is an alef, chet, heh, ayin, or resh are vocalized like yechavet when conjugated in the nifal. The following are examples of each one of the aforementioned: ye’atzer (treasured) and yechasen (laid up) in it shall not be treasured nor laid up (Is. 23:18); yehareg (killed) as in ve-lo yehareg (and will not be killed); ye’aved (plowed) in neither be plowed (Devarim 21:4); yera’eh (appear) in and they shall not appear (Deut,. 16:16), for this is the rule.

Thou shalt not go over the boughs again. Lo tefa’er (Thou shalt not go over the boughs) means you shall not seek after its “glory,” that is, after its branches. Compare, pore’ot (sprigs) in And shot forth sprigs (Yechezkel 17:6). It too is spelled with an alef even though it is read as if written with a vav. Compare, nodot (wineskins) in and wineskins, worn (Yehoshua 9:4).
And thou shalt remember. This is connected to for the stranger (v. 21).
And…judge them. U-shefatum is to be rendered, and the judges judge them. Our verse is similar to No man shall take the mill or the upper millstone to pledge (Devarim 24:6).

Deserve to be beaten. The word bin (deserve) is vocalized with a chirik. Compare, bin nun (son of Nun) (Yehoshua 1:1) and bin yakeh (son of Yake) (Mishlei 30:1). Bin hakkot (deserve to be beaten) is similar to ben bliyya’al (a base fellow) (Shmuel I 25:17). Bin laylah (in a night) in which came up in a night (Yonah 4:10) is similar. The judge is obligated to beat him. I believe that Scripture calls the culprit wicked because he struck his neighbor.
That the judge shall cause him to lie down. By command. The same applies to and to be beaten, as before his face proves.

According to the measure of his wickedness, by number. Of blows. It would have appeared to us, were it not for the words of tradition, that there are some sins that a person is punished for with ten blows. Others are punished with twenty blows. Other sins are punished with a lesser or greater number. The clause according to the measure of his wickedness is proof of this. In any case, the blows shall not exceed forty. However, the words of tradition alone are true. Others say that his wickedness refers to greater or lesser blows, all of which number forty.

Then thy brother should be dishonored. For the thing is well known. It is a decree from the Almighty that the sufferer suffer forty blows. This is a decree from heaven so that the number of blows not depend on the will of the judge.
[When he treadeth.] The deniers say that the bet in be-disho (when he treadeth down) indicates prior to treading. However, this is unnecessary.

If brethren dwell together. The deniers also say that these brethren are not actual brothers, but are relatives. They brought proof from Boaz. However, they contribute nothing, for there is no mention of levirate marriage, only of redemption. Why mention the word together? Does it matter if they were in one state or in one courtyard, or if they loved each other? They say, look, the verse says ve-yibbemah (and shall perform the duty of a husband’s brother unto her). This shows that he is her brother-in-law in name only. It is like thy sister-in-law (yevimtekh) is gone back (Rut 1:15). Now observe that they have become foolish and stupid, for Scripture states, with regard to the sons of Yehudah, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother (ve-yabbem) unto her (Bereshit 38:8). Now he was her brother-in-law. Also, the term yevimtekh (thy sister-in-law) (Rut 1:15) was used because they were married to two brothers. All intelligent people know that the negative commandments given to Moshe were not previously prohibited. However, it would not have been evil in the eyes of Hashem if someone abstained from them before the law was given to Moshe. The fact that Scripture states, for all these abominations have the men of the land done, that were before you (Vayikra 18:27), shows that this is certainly the case. We do not find a prophet who warned them. Look, Scripture says of Onan, who did not give seed to his brother, the thing which he did was evil in the sight of Hashem (Bereshit 38:10). We will therefore rely on the tradition that they are actual brothers.
And have no child. For if the deceased has a son, there is no need for him to take his brother’s wife, for she is forbidden to him.
The word yachdav (together) is to be understood in accordance with the explanation of the transmitters of tradition.
One not of his kin. This explains the term ha-chutzah (abroad). This law applies only if the brother-in-law intends to marry her.
The first-born that she beareth. Will be called by the name of his brother.
That his name be not blotted out. Scripture speaks of his inheritance. I have previously explained the meaning of that she beareth in my comments on unto a foreign people (Shemot 21:8).
My husband’s brother. The yod of yevami (my husband’s brother) is in fact the sign of the object.
And if he stand, and say. Until the elders hear.
And loose. Ve-chaletzah (and loose) is similar to chaletzu (draw out) in draw out the breast (Eichah 3:4). Its meaning is to remove.

In his face. The transmitters of tradition explain that the word be-fanav (in his face) has the meaning of before his face. According to its plain meaning, be-fanav means before the shoe, for panav here is similar to panim (in front) in front and on the back (Yechezkel 2:9).
When men strive. The reverse of If brethren dwell together (v. 5). The men spoken of are strangers or brothers.

By the secrets. Mevushav (the secrets) means his testicles. It is related to the word bushah (shame). It is an act of audacity to uncover that which is hidden, namely, a person’s nakedness. It is also a vital organ.
Then thou shalt cut off her hand. If she does not pay ransom money. Its meaning is similar to eye for eye (Shemot 21:24).
Thine eye shall have no pity. If she be poor.

In thy bag. Where you place the scales. Or, do not deceitfully take the weights from the bag. The first interpretation is correct. The proof text is, Let us all have one hag (kis) (Mishlei 1:14), the meaning of which is, one scale. The word kis (bag) is related to the word tachossu (ye shall make your count) in ye shall make your count for the lamb (Shemot 12:4) even though tachossu comes from a different root. Many explained the word kis to mean a pouch. There is no need for this interpretation.
Perfect. No part shall be missing.
[Just measure.] A just measure means a measure which conforms to the market measure.
That thy days may be long. For it is well known that all righteous kingdoms will endure, for righteousness is like a building. However, unrighteousness is like a ruin. Its wall collapses in a moment

For all that do such things. Those who possess diverse measures and diverse weights. This is followed by a general rule, namely, even all that do unrighteously verbally and by deed, secretly or publicly.
How he met thee. Karekha (met thee) is related to the word korot (befallen) in all that had befallen them (Bereshit 42:29).

And smote the hindmost of thee. Va-yezanev bekhah (and smote the hindmost of thee) means, and cut off your tail (zanav), namely, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, that is, those who did not have the strength to walk. It is possible that the word necheshalim (enfeebled) is similar to nechelashim (enfeebled). Similarly keves (lamb) and kesev (lamb).
When thou was faint. For Amalek came to Refidim where the people thirsted for water. The latter is clearly stated.
And weary. From the way.

And he feared not. This refers to Amalek. Yare (feared) is a verb in the perfect. It is like the word kaved (heavy) in for the thing is too heavy for thee (Shemot 18:8); zaken (old) in that when Yitzchak was old (Bereshit 27:1), and ahev (loveth) in such as he loveth (Ibid., 8).

When Hashem thy Elokim hath given thee rest. It means that this commandment takes effect after Yisrael inherits the land and the land is quiet from all the wars with the surrounding nations, for as long as they are involved in waging war with the nations close to them they are not obligated to fight Amalek.

That thou shalt blot out the remembrance. Namely, slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass (Shmuel I 15:3), so that no one says this ox is from the spoil taken from Amalek. The words of the Torah are a general statement. The words of the prophet Shmuel go into detail.
Thou shalt not forget. Scripture says this after having already stated Remember…(v. 17) for emphasis. The same is true with many other commandments in the Torah.

And it shall be, when thou art come. Since Scripture wrote, Therefore it shall be, when Hashem thy Hashem hath given thee rest (Devarim 25:19), Hashem now says that there are commandments that must be observed before He gives you rest. In fact, these commandments take effect as soon as you enter the land. They are: the first fruits, the tithes, writing the Torah on the stones, building the altar, and the blessing and the curse on the two mountains.

In a basket. Tene (basket) is a basket-like receptacle. The word tanakha (thy basket) (Devarim 28:5) is its companion. This commandment is incumbent upon those who are close to the place of the sanctuary.
[That shall be in those days.] In those days means that this law is in force as long as there is a kohen gadol there.
I profess. The reason for this utterance is so that the children will hear. Or it is, like a statement of thanks to Hashem, for He has fulfilled his oath. The fruit is proof of this.

And thou shalt speak. It is possible that the kohanim will ask, “What is this that you brought?” Hence Scripture reads ve-anita (and thou shalt speak). On the other hand, ve-anita may mean, and you shall begin speaking. Compare, And Iyov spoke (va-ya’an) and said (Iyov 3:2).

A wandering Arami. The word oved (wandering) is an intransitive verb. If Arami referred to Lavan then Scripture should have read mavid or me’abbed. Furthermore, what reason would Scripture have had for stating, Lavan sought to destroy my father and he went down to Mitzrayim? Lavan did not cause Yaakov to descend to Mitzrayim. It thus appears to me that the term Arami refers to Yaakov. Scripture, as it were, reads, when my father was in Aram he was “perishing.” That is, he was poor, he had no money. Similarly oved (perish) in Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish (Mishlei 31:6). Let him drink, and forget his poverty (Mishlei 31:7) is proof. The meaning of our phrase thus is, a perishing Arami was my father. Its import is, I did not inherit the land from my father, for my father was poor when he came to Aram.
